title: Meat and milk (Exodus 23:19)
hook: "thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk" grew into separate dishes and waiting times

segments.voice: Yesterday, which animals: split hooves and chewing the cud, fins and scales. Your line was read the label. What surprised you in the ingredients? Day one hundred forty-six.

Open the kitchen cabinets in a home that keeps kosher, and you might think they own twice as many dishes as they need. Two sets of plates. Two sets of pots. Two sets of silverware, sometimes with colored handles, red for one, blue for the other. Sometimes two sinks. And ask someone there if they want ice cream after a burger, and they might check the clock first. It all grows out of one short sentence in the Torah. A sentence about a baby goat.
screen: `TWO SETS OF DISHES.` → `RED HANDLES, BLUE HANDLES.` → `CHECKING THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The sentence is: "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk." Seethe means boil, and a kid is a young goat. It's an oddly specific rule. And it appears in the Torah not once but three times, twice in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy. The rabbis took that repetition seriously. They taught that three mentions meant three prohibitions: don't cook meat and milk together, don't eat them together, and don't benefit from the mixture, like selling it. Then they widened it. Not just a goat and its own mother's milk, but any meat and any dairy. And by rabbinic law, poultry was included as meat too. Fish and eggs are neither; they're called pareve, neutral, and can go with either. From there come the separate dishes, since pots and pans can absorb flavors. And the waiting times: after eating meat, many Jews wait before eating dairy. How long depends on your family's custom. Many Jews of Eastern European background wait six hours. Many of German background wait three. Jews from the Netherlands traditionally wait one. All are respected traditions. Why this rule at all? The Torah doesn't say. Some commentators suggested it was to keep away from an ancient pagan practice. Others heard compassion in it: the milk that was meant to give a young animal life shouldn't be used to cook it. Here's a lovely puzzle the rabbis noticed: when Abraham hosts three visitors in Genesis, he serves them curd, milk and a calf, all at once. Different sages gave different answers to how that fits. They didn't hide the question.
screen: `A KID IN ITS MOTHER'S MILK.` · `THREE TIMES, THREE RULES.` · `SEPARATE DISHES, WAITING TIMES.` · `A PAGAN PRACTICE, OR COMPASSION?` · then, large: `SOME THINGS STAY APART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait before a second helping. At your next meal, when you're about to go back for more, pause. For now, rehearse it. Settle, and breathe. Picture the plate in front of you, empty. Notice what the wanting feels like, right in the body. Then just wait. Not to punish yourself. To see the space between one thing and the next. The bell holds the time.
Meat and milk. One Torah verse, said three times, that grew into separate dishes, waiting times and a kitchen with two sides.
Your line: some things stay apart. Today, keep two things in your life separate on purpose: work and dinner, the phone and the bed. Day one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher don't cook or eat meat (including poultry) with dairy, keep separate dishes and utensils for each, and wait between meat and dairy according to family custom, often one, three or six hours.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 23:19b ('Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk').
Poultry as rabbinic extension: Mishnah Chullin 8:1 and Chullin 104b (R. Akiva vs. R. Yose HaGelili). Confirm.
Waiting customs: six (many Eastern European), three (many German), one (Dutch). Generalizations; confirm.
Reasons: Maimonides (Guide 3:48) links it to idolatrous practice and also mentions it; compassion reading from other commentators (e.g. Ibn Ezra). Confirm attribution.
Abraham's meal (Genesis 18:8) and rabbinic answers mentioned without detail.
